summary: This RFC defines an XML-based data model for conference objects in centralized conferencing (XCON), which RFC 5239 describes as participants associated with a central focus. The model carries information about a conference and about who takes part in it. Other XCON protocols build on it.

plainLanguage.summary: A conference call needs one document that describes it: who is taking part, when it runs, which media it uses, who may join and who holds the floor. This RFC defines that document as an XML format, called a conference object. It extends the format that SIP already had for conference state, adding schedule, media controls and floor control, so that the description no longer depends on which signalling protocol the conference uses.

questions: what is the xcon conference object
what is the conference information data model
subtitle: The XML document format that describes a centralized conference: its schedule, media, floors and participants.

tldr.problem: A conference call has to be described in a form every program in the system can read: who is in it, when it runs, what media it uses, who may join, and who holds the floor. The SIP event package for conference state already defined a format, but it was tied to SIP and had nothing to describe floor control.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an XML data model for the conference object, extending the existing format with scheduling elements, media control elements, floor control elements and non-SIP URIs, and giving the conference and its participants their own URI schemes. A RELAX NG schema in Section 5 is the normative description.
tldr.outcome: The same document can now describe a conference regardless of the signalling protocol underneath, so a system that runs SIP for sessions and BFCP for floors has one format for both.

today: RFC 6501 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It registers the schema, the XML namespace and the two URI schemes, and it is the data model that the other centralized conferencing specifications build on.

sections.title: What the Document Has to Describe
sections.content:
There is a core set of conference information used in any conference, whatever the media involved. That set is the conference information data model, and this RFC defines it in an XML format. The model is logically represented by the conference object, which is the instantiation of the model for one particular conference. Conference objects are a fundamental concept in centralized conferencing, as described in the framework in RFC 5239, where a conference is defined as an association of participants with a central focus.

The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) event package for conference state, specified in RFC 4575, already defines a data format for conferences. That model is SIP specific, and it lacks elements for some of the functionality in the centralized conferencing framework, floor control among them. The model defined here is a superset of the format in RFC 4575: it supports more call signalling protocols than SIP, and it covers all the functionality of the framework. The extensions include scheduling elements, media control elements, floor control elements, non-SIP URIs, and localization extensions to text elements. The RFC expects that the model can be extended further in future to implement additional advanced features.
sections.plainLanguage:
Every conference has some facts in common: when it runs, who is in it, what can be used to join, and who is allowed to speak. This RFC puts those facts in one XML document, called a conference object, so that every program in the system reads them the same way.

SIP already had a format for describing a conference, but it only covered what SIP needs and had nothing about floor control. This one is a larger version that adds scheduling, media controls and floor control, and does not assume SIP underneath.

sections.title: Format, Namespace and the Conference Identifier
sections.content:
A conference object document is an XML document. It MUST be based on XML 1.0 and MUST be encoded using UTF-8. The normative description of its syntax, for implementers of parsers and generators, is the RELAX NG schema in Section 5, and compliant messages MUST meet the requirements of that schema. The schema is backwards compatible with the framework in RFC 5239, so valid instance documents of that framework are also valid under this schema.

The RFC defines a new namespace for the elements it introduces, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xcon-conference-info, and registers the schema itself at urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:xcon-conference-info.

The conference object identifier, written XCON-URI, can be seen as the key used to access a particular conference object. The conference control protocol uses it to access, manipulate and delete the object, and the conferencing client receives it from the conference notification service or out of band. Its syntax is defined by ABNF: XCON-URI = 'xcon' ':' [conf-object-id '@'] host, where conf-object-id = 1*( unreserved / '+' / '=' / '/' ). An XCON-URI is not designed to be resolved, and an application MUST NOT attempt a standard DNS lookup on the host part to discover an address or port. To compare two identifiers, all components MUST be converted to lowercase and the comparison applied character by character, as in Section 6.2.1 of RFC 3986. The host part serves only as an identifier and is never used as an address, so the same comparison applies even when it is written as an IP address.

The identifier acts as the top-level key in the conferencing system, with the identifiers of the other protocols hanging off it. Figure 1 of the RFC shows a single XCON-URI above the conference identifiers used by call signalling protocols and the 'conference ID' used by BFCP for floor control, which maps one to one with the XCON-URI. The mappings to the other protocols are not strictly one to one, because several signalling protocols may each have a representation linked to the same conference object. The RFC notes that a conferencing system is free to structure these relationships as it requires, and that the figure is a guideline.
sections.plainLanguage:
The document is XML, encoded in UTF-8, and its exact grammar is given as a RELAX NG schema in Section 5. Anything that does not match the schema is not a valid conference object. The elements this RFC adds live in their own XML namespace, so they never clash with the ones from the older SIP format.

Each conference has an identifier of its own, of the form xcon:something@host. It works like a key: the control protocol uses it to fetch, change or delete the conference object. It is not a web address and must not be looked up with DNS. Two identifiers are the same only if their lower-cased forms match character for character.

sections.title: The Structure of the Document
sections.content:
All the information about a conference sits inside a <conference-info> element, which is the root of the document and is defined in RFC 4575. The 'state' and 'version' attributes of that element are not used in this context, because they apply only to notification mechanisms, and this RFC extends the meaning of the 'entity' attribute from a SIP URI to the conference object identifier.

The root element has six child elements. <conference-description> describes the conference as a whole, including its URI, the maximum number of users allowed, the media available and the time the conference starts. <host-info> holds information about the entity hosting the conference, such as its URI. <conference-state> tells subscribers about changes in the overall conference information, and carries the user count, whether the conference is active, whether it is locked, and a new <allow-conference-event-subscription> flag that tells the focus whether to accept a subscription to conference state events; when that flag is absent it defaults to true.

<floor-information> holds the status of the different floors in the conference. <users> describes the membership as a whole and contains a set of <user> elements, one per participant. Finally, when a participant in the main conference joins a sidebar, a new element is created in the conference referenced from <sidebars-by-ref> or under one of the <sidebars-by-val> elements.

The schema allows any element and any attribute to be added wherever it says it can, which is how later specifications extend the model. Elements and attributes from unknown namespaces MUST be ignored, so a reader that does not understand an extension can still read the rest of the document. Section 7 of the RFC gives a complete worked example: a weekly conference with three participants, one administrator, one moderator and one participant, with sidebars allowed, one sidebar, and two floors carrying the audio and video.
sections.plainLanguage:
The document has one top-level element with six parts under it. One describes the conference itself: its name, its address, its schedule, its media and the rules about who may join. One names the host. One holds the current state, such as how many people are connected. One holds the floor information. One lists the participants. One holds the sidebars, which are smaller breakaway conferences.

The grammar allows other elements to be added later without breaking anything, and a reader that meets an element it does not know ignores it and carries on.

sections.title: The Conference Description: Schedule, Addresses and Media
sections.content:
The <conference-description> element is defined in RFC 4575 and describes the conference as a whole. It SHOULD have a 'lang' attribute naming the language used in its contents. It is made up of <language>, <display-text>, <subject>, <free-text>, <keywords>, <allow-sidebars>, <cloning-parent>, <sidebar-parent>, <conference-time>, <conf-uris>, <service-uris>, <maximum-user-count> and <available-media>.

The <language> element names the predominant language expected in the conference, using the values of the Language Subtag Registry. It does not enforce the language: it only tells participants which language is preferred, and they are free to switch. The <allow-sidebars> element is a boolean: true or 1 allows sidebar conferences to be created, and absent, false or 0 does not. The <cloning-parent> and <sidebar-parent> elements carry the XCON-URI of a parent conference, and their presence says that this conference object is a clone of, or a sidebar of, that parent.

The <conference-time> element holds the timing, policy and duration of a conference as one or more <entry> elements, each describing one occurrence. It differs from the iCalendar objects of RFC 5545 in that it can set different policies for the same conference at different times. Each entry holds a <base> element with the iCalendar object, a <mixing-start-offset> and a <mixing-end-offset> that say when media mixing starts and stops, a <can-join-after-offset> and a <must-join-before-offset> that bound when users may join, a <request-user> element, a <notify-end-of-conference> element giving the number of seconds before the end at which the system MUST send a notification, and an <allowed-extend-mixing-end-offset> flag saying whether the conference may be extended. Both offset elements MUST carry a 'required-participant' attribute, whose value is one of none, administrator, moderator, user, observer or participant. It lets a privileged user set the mixing start from the later of the stated time and the arrival of the first participant, and the mixing end from the earlier of the stated time and the departure of the last one.

The <conf-uris> element holds a set of entries, each of which may now carry a <conference-password> element with the password of the conference, for instance the PIN code of a telephone conference. The password element MUST NOT appear in elements of type uris-type other than <conf-uris>.

The <available-media> element lists the media of the conference as entries, each with a display text, a type and a status, plus a <mixing-mode> giving the default scheduling policy the mixer uses to build the outgoing stream, which MUST be one of moderator-controlled, FCFS or automatic; a <codecs> element listing the allowed codecs, with a decision attribute saying whether the focus picks the common codec automatically or needs the moderator's approval; and a <controls> element with the basic global controls: <mute>, <pause-video>, <gain>, whose integer value ranges from -127 to 127, and <video-layout>, which chooses how the video is arranged for each participant. The layout types are single-view, dual-view, dual-view-crop, dual-view-2x1, dual-view-2x1-crop, quad-view, multiple-3x3, multiple-4x4, multiple-5x1 and automatic, and the default is single-view.
sections.plainLanguage:
This part of the document describes the conference itself. It names the language people are expected to use, whether sidebars are allowed, and where the conference came from if it was copied from another one.

The schedule is the most detailed part. Each occurrence of the conference carries a calendar entry and a set of times: when media mixing starts and stops, the window in which people may still join, and how long before the end to warn people. The mixing times also say who has to be present for them to count, so a moderator can hold the start until they arrive.

The media part says which audio and video streams exist, which codecs are allowed, and the global controls a moderator has: mute, pause video, gain and the layout of the video.

sections.title: Floor Control: Who Is Allowed to Speak
sections.content:
The <floor-information> element holds the <conference-ID>, <allow-floor-events>, <floor-request-handling> and <conference-floor-policy> child elements. The absence of the whole element means that the conference does not have a floor at all.

The <conference-ID> represents a conference instance within floor control. When BFCP is the floor control protocol it is a 32-bit BFCP conference identifier as defined in RFC 4582, and it maps one to one with the conference object identifier.

The <allow-floor-events> element is a boolean action. If true, the focus is instructed to accept a subscription to floor control events; if false it rejects the subscription; if it is undefined the default is false, so the subscription is rejected. A participant can subscribe in two ways: an offer and answer exchange using SIP INVITE with BFCP parameters in the SDP, or the general authorization mechanism in Section 9 of RFC 4582 and RFC 5018.

The <floor-request-handling> element says what the focus does with a request for a floor. The value 'block' denies the request and is the default. The value 'confirm' allows the request, and the focus then uses the defined floor algorithm to allow or deny it; the algorithms themselves are outside the scope of the RFC.

The <conference-floor-policy> element holds one or more <floor> elements, each with an 'id' attribute that uniquely identifies the floor within the conference and, for BFCP, corresponds to the floor-id identifier. Every floor has one or more mandatory <media-label> elements, and the number of them says how many floors the conference can have; where <available-media> is present, the label MUST equal the label of the corresponding media stream entry. A floor has a mandatory <algorithm> element, set to moderator-controlled, FCFS or random, an optional <max-floor-users> element limiting how many users may hold the floor at one time, and an optional <moderator-id> element naming the moderator, which MUST be set when the algorithm is moderator-controlled. A participant who needs to talk first has to get the floor from the chair of the conference.
sections.plainLanguage:
Floor control is the part that decides who is allowed to speak at a time. The document can be entirely absent when the conference has no floor.

It names the floor in the protocol's own terms, says whether participants may subscribe to floor events, and says what the server should do when someone asks for the floor: refuse it, which is the default, or accept the request and let the floor's own algorithm decide.

Each floor then says which media streams it covers, which decides how many floors the conference has, how the floor is handed around, by moderator, first come first served or at random, and how many people may hold it at once.

sections.title: Identifying the Participants
sections.content:
The <user> element describes one participant. Its 'entity' attribute holds a unique conference user identifier, the XCON-USERID, which is unique within the scope of the conference. The syntax is defined by ABNF: XCON-USERID = 'xcon-userid' ':' conf-user-id, where conf-user-id = 1*unreserved. As with the XCON-URI, all components MUST be converted to lowercase before comparison, and the comparison is then applied codepoint by codepoint after conversion to a common character encoding.

Other user identifiers can be associated with the conference user identifier so that the conferencing system can map several authenticated identities onto one global identifier. Figure 2 of the RFC shows a conference user identifier above the BFCP user ID, the SIP user URI and the H323 user URI that belong to the same person. A conferencing system is free to structure these relationships as it requires, and the figure is a guideline.

The <user> element contains <display-text>, <associated-aors>, <provide-anonymity>, <roles>, <languages>, <cascaded-focus>, <allow-refer-users-dynamically>, <allow-invite-users-dynamically>, <allow-remove-users-dynamically> and <endpoint>. The <roles> element carries one or more of administrator, moderator, user, participant, observer or none, where none means any role is assigned; the meaning of the roles is out of scope and left to future policy documents.

The <provide-anonymity> element says how much anonymity the server should give the user. The real user information stays in the data model but SHOULD NOT be provided to the other participants. There are three values: private, meaning the user is completely anonymous; semi-private, meaning the user is anonymous to everyone who has not been given permission to see them; and hidden, meaning other users cannot see the participant in the conference at all.

The three 'allow' elements are booleans that say whether a participant may ask the focus to refer a user to the conference, to invite a user, or to remove a user, without changing the allowed users list. When the element is undefined the value is false and the request is rejected.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each participant is identified inside the conference by an identifier of their own, of the form xcon-userid:name. It is unique within that one conference. The same person may be known by several different addresses in other protocols, such as SIP and BFCP, and the system keeps a mapping between them and the single conference identifier.

A participant also has roles, which say what they are allowed to do, and an anonymity setting that decides how much of that participant the other participants can see.

sections.title: Who May Join the Conference
sections.content:
The <users> element contains <join-handling>, <user-admission-policy>, <allowed-users-list>, <deny-users-list> and the <user> elements.

The <join-handling> element says what the focus does with a request to join. The values are 'block', which denies access and is the default; 'confirm', which puts the participant on a pending list, for example by parking the call on a music-on-hold server, while waiting for the moderator; 'allow', which accepts the request and grants access; 'authenticate', which requires a combination of username and password; and 'directed-operator', which directs the user to an operator.

The <user-admission-policy> lets an organizer, or a participant with the right to do so, choose how users are authenticated into the conference, using a mechanism of the conference's choosing. Three values are defined. A 'closedAuthenticated' policy requires each participant to be on the allowed users list and to be sufficiently authenticated, and requests from anyone else are rejected unless a join-handling action of 'confirm' is chosen; it MUST NOT include a deny users list, and if one appears it MUST be ignored. An 'openAuthenticated' policy requires every participant to be authenticated, typically meaning anyone who can authenticate with the conferencing system may join, and it SHOULD have a deny users list so that participants can be banned until they are un-banned; it MUST NOT include an allowed users list, and if one appears it MUST be ignored. An 'anonymous' policy grants any join request and is the least restrictive; it MUST NOT include either list, and if either appears it MUST be ignored. In all other cases the appearance of both lists MUST be ignored, except as a future specification may describe otherwise.

The <allowed-users-list> holds a list of user URIs, roles or domains that the focus uses to decide who can join, who can be invited, and who the focus needs to refer to the conference. It contains zero or more <target> elements, each with a mandatory 'uri' attribute and a mandatory 'method' attribute. The method is one of 'dial-in', which lists who can join; 'dial-out', which lists the resources with which the focus will initiate a session; and 'refer', which lists the resources the focus needs to refer to the conference, where the resource is expected to start the session itself. The same URI may appear more than once with different methods, and different users may have different access rights to the lists, which is why the methods are separated. The list also has a <persistent-list> child element, which stores information about users who are not currently part of a session: their name, nickname, conference user identifier and email address.

The <deny-users-list> holds the URIs, roles or domains of the users who have been banned. Such users cannot rejoin until the ban is lifted.
sections.plainLanguage:
The document says what happens when someone tries to join. The focus can refuse the request, which is the default, park the caller on hold while a moderator decides, let them in, ask for a username and password, or pass them to an operator.

It also says who is allowed in. A closed conference lists the people on its guest list and requires each to prove who they are. An open conference lets anyone who can authenticate join, but keeps a list of people who are banned until they are let back in. An anonymous conference lets anyone in and keeps no lists at all.

Each entry on the guest list says not only who, but how: whether they dial in, whether the conference calls them, or whether they are asked to join.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The overall security considerations for authentication and for the security and privacy of identity in Sections 11 and 11.2 of the framework in RFC 5239 apply to this document. Because this specification defines a data model rather than a protocol, each protocol that provides access to conference objects has to discuss how it meets the requirements set out here.

A conferencing system usually supports several protocols, for example SIP for session control and BFCP for floor control, and each may use its own authentication mechanism. Where a user is authenticated by more than one mechanism, it is up to the conferencing system to map all of them to the same user.

Users may also use different identifiers to reach a conference, and the system keeps a mapping database from those authenticated namespaces to the XCON-USERID. Several threats apply to that database. The administrator of the conferencing system MUST ensure that only authorized users can connect to it, for example with access control rules, and its integrity MUST be protected against unauthorized modification. The XCON-USERID or XCON-URI SHOULD be hard to guess, and it is critical that the URI remain difficult to guess by brute force. It is RECOMMENDED that the database use encryption if the information is kept in long-term storage, that the confidentiality of the database be protected if it contains sensitive elements such as passwords, and that access is offered only over encrypted channels such as TLS. Administrators SHOULD also avoid disclosing information to unauthorized parties when a conference is cloned or a sidebar is created, since an external sidebar may include participants who were not authorized for the parent conference. The security considerations for the SIP REFER method in Section 5.2 of RFC 3515 also apply. The specification of a privacy policy is outside the scope of the document, but a privacy policy will be needed in a real implementation.
sections.plainLanguage:
The document defines a format, not a protocol, so the rules for who may read a conference object, and who may change it, have to be set by each protocol that carries it.

One area gets particular attention: the database that maps a person's different addresses onto one conference identifier. Only authorised users may reach it, and nobody may change it without permission. The identifiers themselves should be hard to guess, so that they cannot be found by trying enough combinations.

viz.caption: THE TWO IDENTIFIER SYNTAXES, AS DEFINED IN THE RFC

data.title: XCON-URI and XCON-USERID
data.code:
XCON-URI = "xcon" ":" [conf-object-id "@"] host
conf-object-id = 1*( unreserved / "+" / "=" / "/" )

XCON-USERID = "xcon-userid" ":" conf-user-id
conf-user-id = 1*unreserved

cells: Only the participants on the allowed users list, and each must be authenticated
The allowed users list is used; a deny users list must be ignored
Anyone who can authenticate with the conferencing system
A deny users list is expected for bans; an allowed users list must be ignored
Neither list may be used; both must be ignored

viz.caption: THE VALUES THAT GOVERN THE FLOOR AND THE MIXING

items.label: Floor request denied
items.desc: The focus denies the floor request. This is the default action.

items.label: Allowed, then decided
items.desc: The focus allows the request and then uses the floor algorithm to allow or deny it.

items.label: The moderator decides
items.desc: As a mixing mode, the moderator controls the media stream policy; as a floor algorithm, the moderator controls the floor.

items.label: First come, first served
items.desc: The floor or the stream is granted in the order it is requested.

items.label: Random
items.desc: A floor algorithm value that hands the floor over at random.

items.label: The focus chooses
items.desc: A mixing mode value meaning the mixer must choose the best scheduling policy for the conference.
